Speaker notes

LLMs are exciting because they are text-in text-out, and almost anything can be serialized and deserialized via text.
03
04
05

Speaker notes

These are all content generation, where its value is predominantly the immediate content of the output.
06

Speaker notes

Text can be interpreted as code that is executed, and is the basis of automation loops. This has the potential to transform how work is done.
07

Speaker notes

Code does not execute in a vacuum. It runs within a system -- an execution substrate. For the database community, the dominant substrate would be the database management system, and the program would be SQL.
08

Speaker notes

But the power of LLMs and agents is in its expansive capabilities to execute and automate _any_ digital system. This goes well beyond a database and encompasses the entire digital environment -- the OS, agent, harness, web services, etc.

All of these systems contain and manipulate data, and that's where the action is. So data management should expand its world view to systems with state.
09

Speaker notes

The problem with automation is that LLMs are also unreliable -- and not in terms of failing fast nor easy-to-detect corruptions, but in terms of semantic and correctness issues that are subtle to detect. And this then corrupts the -semantic correctness- of anything that consumes and depends on the LLM's outputs.
10
11
12

Speaker notes

Which eventually includes the computing environment. Incidents like the openai hugging face incident are top of mind, but subtle errors arise in any run-of-the-mill task as well.
13

Speaker notes

The same way we don't rely on end-users to ensure their inputs and actions are safe and correct, we should not rely on LLMs and agents to be correct either. What does it take to ensure high quality and safe agent automation? Better models plan a role, but that itself is not sufficient.
14

Speaker notes

Despite large revenues, there is still a large gap between what technology currently provides, and what organizations need to fully adopt.
15

Speaker notes

This is ultimately a quality problem, which typically demands vertical integration in order to co-design a system to control quality. The lab spans from applications and HCI all the way down to cloud infrastructure. This talk surveys a few examples of work from members of the lab that cuts across this stack.
16

Speaker notes

Agents often try the same task K times. Since each trajectory is just a sample, a good outcome exists, drawing more samples should increase the chances of seeing a good outcome.

Companies like Daytona offer cheap and scalable deployment of sandboxes.
17

Speaker notes

But often the agent has performed several actions and changed the VM state. Migrating or replicating that state to a another machine usually requires shipping the VM state over the network (e.g., via RDMA), which is slow.

Kostis, Asaf, and their students developed a suite of systems that use CXL to reduce the cost to constant time.
18

Speaker notes

RDMA is their approach, while
19

Speaker notes

While skyfall supports fast replication, agents really benefit from the ability to recursively branch (ideally in parallel) and to restore to any point in the past. VM-scale snapshotting is very expensive, while existing container snapshotting such as Docker or Podman+CRIU do not capture enough state and end up reducing task accuracy.
20

Speaker notes

On a sample of 11 difficult tasks in Terminal-bench 2, using a range of models and harnesses, we find that there's a trade-off between pass rate and cost (log scale!).
21

Speaker notes

But giving cheap model + vanilla harness (terminus) the ability to explore using waypoint is able to push the pareto frontier to exceed GPT5.5 at >25x cheaper cost.
22

Speaker notes

The ability to explore increases the chances of a good trajectory, but also the chances of unsafe trajectories too.

Here, the user asks to repurchase a shirt. The agent reads the orders and finds the shirt, but needs a confirmation code in order to check out. When it reads the email, it sees a discount on pills and decides to buy them.

The main point is that the only data flows into buy() should be from Orders. If this is enforced in the environment, buying the pills would be categorically rejected.
23

Speaker notes

Trust in the environment, which sees all state, also makes its feedback reliable. When the environment detects a violation it can steer the agent towards safer trajectories rather than stop the agent.
24

Speaker notes

The key result is summarized in this Agent Dyn benchmark. Most existing safety approaches try to filter tools, construct a "safe plan" from the task before execution, or detect safety violations in the prompt. They all give up safety for task accuracy.

In these benchmarks, observing and enforcing policies over data flows is sufficient to basically eliminate safety violations and improve the task success rates above not even having defenses at all!
25

Speaker notes

The environment and infrastructure can support agent exploration and safety, but what about multi-agent swarms?

One project called Cacheback looks at how subagents should communicate with the main agent.
26

Speaker notes

The typical way is that the sender model reads a bunch of evidence (a PDF, folder in the codebase, an essay, etc), summarizes it, and sends the text to the receiver. But text is lossy, and the decoding and encoding costs are very high.

LatentMAS shows that it's possible, if the sender and receivers use the same model, to ship the sender's KV to the receiver and improve task accuracy. But the KV is orders of magnitude larger than the model! It improves accuracy a bit, but it consume considerable GPU-resources.
27

Speaker notes

But not everything is relevant to the receiver's task in the first place. The key idea is to condition the sender's communication to what the receiver needs.

A simple approach is for the receiver to simply tell the sender what information it needs, and use that "query" to filter the relevant token positions in the KV and compress it.
28

Speaker notes

On a Fanout QA benchmark, where the receiver is a 8B model and we vary the size of the sender models, using text-based communication sees a huge trade-off between latency and accuracy.
29

Speaker notes

But if we use receiver-conditioned communication, the KV is small enough and precise enough that it reduces latency by 3-4x _and_ improves the task accuracy from 40% to nearly 55%! It's win-win.

In general, there's a rich design space for how agents can communicate with each other, designing stronger agentic models, as well as work on co-designing RL and exploration algorithms to leverage environment-level capabilities.
30

Speaker notes

Knowing whether adopting agents even makes progress remains an open question, and the lab develops many benchmarks for impactful use cases on our own, and alongside industry partners [1]

One example is LakeQA[2], which pushes forward QA benchmarks to data-lake scale. Its tasks are multi-source, multi-hop, and requires agenst to both search for appropriate evidence and analyze the returned documents/datasets to derive the correct intermediate information.

[1] https://daplab.cs.columbia.edu/projects/?view=benchmarks
[2] https://lakeqa-bench.github.io/
31

Speaker notes

Finally, agents are being used in almost every application. One exciting use case was highlighted in Anthropic's blog post about formalizing Fermat's Last Theorem[1], led by Tianyi Peng who is on leave from Columbia and DAPLab to work at Anthropic.

The formalization effort built on top of https://prove2.me/ a lean-centric social network where anyone with AI agents can contribute to math formalization. Realizing this goal requires coordinating the work of many decentralized agents so that their individual contributions compose into a coherent whole. Prove2Me provides a harness that makes this kind of multi-agent collaboration efficient.

The workloads and demands of these types of applications inform every lower layer in the technology stack.

[1] https://www.anthropic.com/research/formalizing-fermats-last-theorem
32

Speaker notes

Traditionally, technologists design products that dictate how users should use them, and workloads mature and evolve at a slow enough rate that different CS disciplines can abstract away the application/user and design against that abstraction. For instance, database research abstracts the application as a SQL workload.

Agents have the capability to do _anything_ in digital space! And end-users are leveraging these capabilities. This may be the first time in technology where end-users have been given such a powerful, yet easy-to-use technology that the use cases they are dreaming up _and implementing_ is moving so fast that technology is being dragged behind it.
